actors.name: Naim Qassem
actors.position: Rejects linking reconstruction to disarmament; calls for state responsibility alongside party assistance.
actors.assessment: December 2024 stresses Hezbollah/Iran assistance. April 2025 explicitly rejects an arms-for-reconstruction link and demands state action. September 2026 combines party housing support with renewed demands on the state. The collected statements do not establish acceptance of disarmament as a reconstruction condition.

actors.name: Hassan Fadlallah
actors.position: Calls for state responsibility and funding for shelter, repairs and rebuilding.
actors.change: More implementation detail; no reversal established
actors.assessment: October 2026 retains the demand for state-funded reconstruction and adds a shelter-programme pledge. His sequence for defence talks concerns security negotiations; it should not be read as a condition for receiving household assistance.

actors.name: Ali Fayyad
actors.role: Hezbollah MP; Loyalty to the Resistance bloc
actors.position: Urges the government to begin rebuilding preparations and support without waiting for foreign aid.
actors.change: Implementation detail increases; very short comparison window
actors.assessment: Statements two days apart in June 2025 move from criticizing inaction to naming initial steps. They support a near-term continuity assessment, not a long-term account of changing views.

actors.name: Nabih Berri
actors.position: Rejects political or military trade-offs for aid; presses for urgent state-led rebuilding.
actors.assessment: The March 2025 rejection of aid-for-weapons bargaining is followed by a November appeal to fund and start reconstruction. The later statement adds implementation pressure; it does not establish a new position on arms conditionality.

actors.name: Ali Hassan Khalil
actors.role: Amal MP; political aide to Nabih Berri
actors.position: Demands prompt state reconstruction and rejects political prices attached to it.
actors.assessment: November calls for resources and restoration. December explicitly rejects political prices. The earlier statement did not specify a position on conditionality, so this is clarification rather than a demonstrated reversal.

actors.name: Inaya Ezzeddine
actors.role: Amal MP; Women and Children Committee chair
actors.position: Demands active state support and rapid rebuilding of southern schools.
actors.assessment: March and June 2025 both stress state responsibility and education recovery. Her references to consensus and teacher fairness are not donor disbursement conditions.

actors.name: Samir Geagea
actors.position: Presents exclusive state control of arms as necessary for reconstruction and recovery.
actors.assessment: April 2025 links recovery to sovereignty and state arms control. September blames delayed weapons collection for delayed reconstruction. July 2026 says rebuilding cannot be achieved before an effective state with one army. These are political arguments and prerequisites, not evidence that he personally controls donor disbursements.

actors.name: Ghassan Hasbani
actors.role: Lebanese Forces MP; Strong Republic bloc
actors.position: Links finance to arms control and security; also calls for Iran to contribute to reconstruction costs.
actors.assessment: May and September 2026 both link financing or investment to resolving the arms issue. The May statement also assigns financial responsibility to Iran; its absence from September is not evidence he abandoned it.

actors.name: Pierre Bou Assi
actors.role: Lebanese Forces MP; Strong Republic bloc
actors.position: Requires state authority and official state channels for international rebuilding assistance.
actors.assessment: One dated reconstruction statement collected. His institutional-channel requirement and sovereignty argument should be kept distinct.

actors.name: Gebran Bassil
actors.role: Party leader / Strong Lebanon bloc leader
actors.position: Rejects arms-linked pressure on reconstruction; demands a defined financing and rebuilding plan.
actors.change: Different conditions; not a proven reversal
actors.assessment: August 2025 includes reconstruction among the gains that should accompany arms handover. October explicitly rejects withholding reconstruction over arms. December objects to a borrowing law for lacking a plan. A demand for reconstruction in a security package, rejection of political pressure, and scrutiny of borrowing can coexist.

actors.name: Ghassan Atallah
actors.position: Criticizes a budget that does not provide for reconstruction.
actors.assessment: One dated reconstruction statement collected. It calls for funding; it does not establish acceptance or rejection of an arms condition. Affiliation is also documented by MTV and SBS reporting in 2025.

actors.name: Samy Gemayel
actors.position: Says Hezbollah’s weapons obstruct aid and reconstruction.
actors.assessment: June 2025 combines his own argument with a claim about what foreign delegations demand. June 2026 repeats the claim that militia weapons block reconstruction and return. The sample shows continuity, not a newly adopted condition.

actors.name: Salim Sayegh
actors.position: Rejects Berri’s claim that aid and weapons can be separated in practice; advocates a civilian transition.
actors.assessment: One dated reconstruction statement collected. He describes expectations of Lebanon’s foreign partners and advocates compliance, rather than publishing a donor agreement.

actors.name: Elias Hankach
actors.position: Links reconstruction to state arms control and transparent aid management; wording on state responsibility varies.
actors.change: Possible change in framing; not a proven reversal
actors.assessment: On 5 March he assigns responsibility to those who brought the war and calls for a transparent grant mechanism. On 22 July he describes reconstruction as a duty the state must perform after asserting control. This may distinguish responsibility for paying from responsibility for administering aid; full broadcast comparison is still needed.

actors.name: Walid Joumblatt
actors.role: Former PSP leader; statement attributed to him personally
actors.position: Links reconstruction to reform.
actors.assessment: Only one reconstruction-specific statement is included. It supports a reform link but cannot establish the party’s full position or a change over time.

actors.name: Timour Joumblatt
actors.position: Supports international reconstruction assistance and an integrated state-security-and-return program.
actors.change: Broader security framework; no reversal established
actors.assessment: January 2025 emphasizes a functioning government and international support. July 2026 explicitly combines a lasting ceasefire, withdrawal, state arms control and reconstruction without specifying that all aid must wait.

actors.name: Tony Frangieh
actors.position: Calls for return and reconstruction to be presidential priorities, alongside diplomacy and army support.
actors.assessment: One dated reconstruction statement collected. Support for state arms control elsewhere in the interview does not establish an explicit precondition for all reconstruction aid.

actors.name: Saad Hariri
actors.role: Future Movement leader; former prime minister
actors.position: Frames reconstruction as a shared national duty and part of rebuilding the state.
actors.assessment: One dated reconstruction passage collected. The speech supports state institutions and Arab ties, but does not explicitly make civilian assistance conditional on disarmament.

actors.name: Bahia Hariri
actors.position: Presents rebuilding as the next task after relief and stresses keeping the South’s land and borders.
actors.assessment: One July 2026 statement collected. It recognizes a long reconstruction effort but does not specify a funding source or an aid prerequisite.

actors.name: Hanna Gharib
actors.position: Demands urgent rebuilding and compensation; links return to ending occupation and resisting external conditions.
actors.change: Continuity with a later negotiation focus
actors.assessment: January calls for rapid rebuilding and adequate compensation. December places return and reconstruction among the aims of indirect security talks, while criticizing coercive conditions. No reversal on rebuilding support is established.

actors.name: Asaad Hardan
actors.role: Identified as SSNP president in the cited Al-Binaa reports
actors.position: Calls for state reconstruction and an end to Israeli attacks; opposes externally imposed disarmament.
actors.assessment: July says attacks prevent rebuilding. August presses the government to act from a position of strength rather than rely on foreign guarantees. No separate reconstruction aid eligibility rule is specified.

actors.name: Camille Chamoun
actors.role: National Liberal Party leader and MP
actors.position: Links reconstruction investment to disarmament and rule of law; supports negotiations with Israel.
actors.change: Added diplomatic emphasis; no reversal established
actors.assessment: July stresses arms control to attract reconstruction investment. December presents negotiations alongside disarmament as the route to rebuilding. These statements add detail rather than reverse the earlier position.

actors.name: Imad al-Hout
actors.position: Expects Arab and Gulf reconstruction assistance, though less than in 2006.
actors.assessment: One December 2024 interview collected. His expectation of aid within a broader institutional recovery is not a documented donor pledge or an explicit aid prerequisite.

actors.name: Hagop Terzian
actors.role: Armenian MPs bloc; Tashnag-backed electoral representative
actors.position: Describes perceived donor pressure; later links return and rebuilding to compliance with the agreement.
actors.assessment: June 2026 distinguishes his inference about conditions from firsthand knowledge. August stresses Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah compliance. Neither excerpt establishes that he controls funding or personally proposes an aid freeze.
actors.affiliationNote: Grouped with Tashnag through electoral and bloc affiliation; formal party membership is not asserted. His statements are not a substitute for the party leadership’s position.

actors.name: Mark Daou
actors.position: Urges reconstruction to proceed in parallel with reforms; describes international security requirements as a separate track.
actors.assessment: December 2024 lists reconstruction, ceasefire implementation and reform as government tasks. March 2025 explicitly opposes suspending reconstruction while appointments and the budget are completed.

actors.name: Faisal Karami
actors.position: Demands fair regional access to rebuilding funds and reconstruction of the South within restored state authority.
actors.assessment: October 2025 demands that neglected Tripoli and the North benefit too. June 2026 focuses on the South, withdrawal and state authority. The later statement does not retract the earlier regional demand.

actors.name: Hassan Mrad
actors.position: Calls for immediate reconstruction and rejects political bargaining over this right.
actors.assessment: December 2024 calls for rebuilding and social recovery. March 2025 explicitly rejects bargaining and political wrangling. The earlier excerpt does not establish a contrary position.

actors.name: Osama Saad
actors.role: Popular Nasserist Organization leader and MP
actors.position: Demands reconstruction and return commitments in the budget, with national dialogue and attention to social needs.
actors.assessment: July 2025 places rebuilding among crises requiring national consensus. January 2026 specifically criticizes missing budget commitments and warns about political costs of foreign aid. No reversal is established.

actors.name: Joseph Aoun
actors.position: Connects reconstruction, state security control and Israeli withdrawal in a broader settlement.
actors.change: More detailed sequencing; no reversal established
actors.assessment: July 2025 describes parallel implementation of a package including arms handover, Israeli withdrawal and a reconstruction conference. July 2026 describes withdrawal, army control and state-run reconstruction as parts of disarmament and reintegration. Reconstruction is an enabling component of that process; this is not simply an instruction to withhold civilian aid until disarmament.

actors.name: Nawaf Salam
actors.position: Rejects political bargaining over aid and argues that return and basic recovery should proceed during crisis.
actors.change: Continuity, with a clearer early-recovery focus
actors.assessment: Earlier statements reject political bargaining over assistance. October 2026 adds rehabilitation tenders, external financing needs and a timetable for reciprocal commitments. These distinct scopes do not establish a reversal on every funding condition.

actors.name: Youssef Raggi
actors.role: Foreign minister, also rendered Joe Rajji in the source
actors.position: Reports external requirements for state arms control and economic reform.
actors.assessment: One interview is included. Raggi reports messages from foreign partners and also endorses state sovereignty. His account should not be treated as a verified universal condition in every donor agreement.

actors.name: Fouad Makhzoumi
actors.position: Demands exclusive state management of reconstruction funds, transparency and independent oversight.
actors.assessment: One September 2026 statement is included. It specifies who should manage reconstruction and places return and rebuilding within a coordinated withdrawal/disarmament process. It is attributed to Makhzoumi, even though published on the Lebanese Forces website after a joint meeting.

actors.name: Najaat Aoun Saliba
actors.role: MP; listed individually pending current party-affiliation verification
actors.position: Calls for opening cement imports and reducing customs charges to make rebuilding possible.
actors.assessment: One September 2026 intervention collected. This is a practical materials-cost proposal, not an explicit political condition on assistance.
actors.affiliationNote: Kept outside Taqaddom’s party comparison: a 2023 report describes suspension of her activity in the party; current membership was not established in this research.

actors.name: France — Foreign ministry
actors.position: Supports a state arms monopoly and reconstruction conferences when conditions permit.
actors.assessment: The statement places reconstruction support in a security and sovereignty context but does not define an exact funding trigger. A strict “no money until complete disarmament” rule cannot be inferred from this wording alone.

actors.name: World Bank — LEAP
actors.position: Publishes project eligibility, prioritization and government implementation arrangements.
actors.change: Project rules; not a party opinion
actors.assessment: The FAQ describes $250 million in initial financing, safeguards and eligible activities. It does not state a Hezbollah-disarmament condition. This observation is limited to the FAQ, not a legal audit of all loan documents or a statement about every donor.

parties.name: Hezbollah
parties.comparison: Qassem rejects arms-linked conditionality. Fadlallah emphasizes shelter and phased state repairs. Ali Fayyad urges initial work without waiting for foreign aid. These are complementary emphases in the sample.

parties.name: Amal
parties.comparison: Berri and Ali Hassan Khalil reject political bargaining over reconstruction. Inaya Ezzeddine emphasizes state protection and rapid school rebuilding. Her education priorities do not establish disagreement over aid conditions.

parties.name: Lebanese Forces
parties.comparison: Geagea, Hasbani and Bou Assi link reconstruction to state authority and arms control. Bou Assi specifies state aid channels; Hasbani additionally demands an Iranian contribution to costs.

parties.name: Free Patriotic Movement
parties.comparison: Bassil rejects arms-linked conditionality but objects to borrowing without a plan. Ghassan Atallah demands a reconstruction budget allocation. Different financing emphases do not by themselves establish disagreement.

parties.name: Kataeb
parties.comparison: Gemayel and Sayegh emphasize arms control and donor confidence. Hankach adds transparency requirements; his March and July descriptions of state responsibility differ and need context before calling a reversal.

parties.name: Progressive Socialist Party
parties.comparison: Walid Joumblatt links reconstruction to reform. Timour Joumblatt calls for international support, later endorsing a package of withdrawal, state arms control, return and reconstruction. Walid is the former party leader.

parties.name: Marada Movement
parties.comparison: Tony Frangieh calls for reconstruction and return as presidential priorities, alongside support for the army and diplomacy. No explicit aid-withholding condition is stated. One speaker only.

parties.name: Future Movement
parties.comparison: Saad Hariri presents rebuilding as a national responsibility; Bahia Hariri emphasizes the long rebuilding task and the South’s territorial integrity. Neither collected excerpt states an explicit aid prerequisite. Different speakers are not a time series for one person.

parties.name: Lebanese Communist Party
parties.comparison: Hanna Gharib demands rapid rebuilding and compensation; later places return and rebuilding among the objectives of indirect security negotiations. One speaker only.

parties.name: Syrian Social Nationalist Party
parties.comparison: Asaad Hardan stresses that Israeli attacks obstruct reconstruction and calls on the government to start rebuilding while rejecting externally imposed disarmament. Only Hardan is represented; other SSNP currents are not covered.

parties.name: National Liberal Party
parties.comparison: Camille Chamoun links investment and rebuilding to disarmament and rule of law, later emphasizing negotiations with Israel as the route to rebuilding. One speaker only.

parties.name: Jamaa Islamiya
parties.comparison: Imad al-Hout expects reconstruction aid and emphasizes institutional recovery. No explicit aid prerequisite appears in the collected excerpt. One speaker and one date only.

parties.name: Tashnag / Armenian MPs affiliation
parties.comparison: Terzian describes perceived donor pressure and later urges agreement compliance to enable return and rebuilding. He is a Tashnag-backed bloc representative; formal membership is not asserted. Party leadership and second-speaker coverage remain missing.

parties.name: Taqaddom
parties.comparison: Mark Daou argues for reconstruction alongside reform rather than waiting for appointments and budget work. His description of security conditions is expressly distinguished from the reconstruction track. One speaker only.

parties.name: Karama Movement
parties.comparison: Faisal Karami demands fair access for Tripoli and the North, then stresses rebuilding the South alongside withdrawal and state authority. These cover different needs, not a demonstrated reversal. One speaker only.

parties.name: Union Party (Al-Ittihad)
parties.comparison: Hassan Mrad calls for rebuilding, then explicitly rejects bargaining over it and demands an immediate start. One speaker only.

parties.name: Popular Nasserist Organization
parties.comparison: Osama Saad links recovery to national dialogue and social needs, then demands budget commitments for rebuilding and return. His concerns about political prices do not identify a specific donor’s terms. One speaker only.

parties.name: Other officials and MPs
parties.comparison: Individual timelines for state officeholders and MPs listed outside party comparisons. An institutional title does not make every remark a cabinet decision. Uncertain current affiliations are flagged on the person’s profile.

parties.name: External context
parties.comparison: Limited contextual sample from France and the World Bank. These two institutions do not represent every donor or funding instrument.

methodology.unit: One dated statement by one named speaker. Attendance alone is not a statement. Party grouping does not convert a personal statement into a formal resolution.
methodology.conditionRule: Separate own prerequisites, reported donor conditions, reciprocal packages, project safeguards, practical obstacles and explicit rejection of conditionality. No condition stated is not the same as unconditional support.
methodology.changeRule: Compare the same speaker and scope. Silence on an earlier condition does not prove abandonment. Single observations cannot establish change.
methodology.coverage: Selected public evidence across 17 party groupings and individual officials/MPs. Seven groupings contain multiple named speakers. Tashnag coverage uses a party-backed bloc representative, with formal membership not asserted.
gaps: Second speakers for Marada, LCP, SSNP, NLP, Jamaa Islamiya, Tashnag, Taqaddom, Karama, Union Party and Popular Nasserist Organization
Lebanese Democratic Party, Arab Tawhid, other unrepresented parties and many independent MPs
Tashnag leadership statements and competing SSNP currents
Longer time series for speakers with one statement, and full broadcasts underlying several reports
methodology.freshness: Selected public statements reviewed through 12 October 2026. Latest collected means the newest entry here, not necessarily the speaker’s latest public position. Announcements do not establish delivery.
